slides.title: 9.1 Linux Storage Architecture
keyPoints: Each layer has its own identity, size, and failure modes. A larger disk does not automatically enlarge its filesystem. A healthy filesystem does not prove the physical storage is reliable.
Linux example — 9.1
Observe disks, partitions, and mounts together.
slides.narration:
A typical path from application data to hardware can include a file, filesystem, logical volume, partition, block device, storage controller, and physical media. Not every system uses every layer. A filesystem can live directly on a block device, and cloud or virtual storage adds layers outside the guest.

Each layer has its own identity, size, and failure modes. A larger disk does not automatically enlarge its filesystem. A healthy filesystem does not prove the physical storage is reliable.

Draw the actual stack before changing it. Use findmnt, lsblk, and, where applicable, LVM tools. Record which layer owns the change requested by the application team. The correct command follows from that model, not from the phrase “add space.”

slides.title: 9.2 Block Devices
keyPoints: A block device exposes addressable storage blocks. Linux paths can include /dev/sda, /dev/vda, or /dev/nvme0n1, depending on the device and driver. Partition names follow device-specific conventions, such as /dev/nvme0n1p1.
These short names can change when hardware discovery order changes. Persistent paths under /dev/disk/by-id and filesystem UUIDs provide more stable references for appropriate tasks.

slides.title: 9.4 blkid
keyPoints: blkid probes block-device metadata and can report filesystem type, UUID, and label. It complements lsblk by identifying recognized on-disk signatures.

A filesystem UUID identifies the filesystem, not necessarily the underlying physical disk. Reformatting creates a new filesystem identity; cloning can copy an existing UUID and create ambiguity when both copies are attached.
Linux example — 9.4
slides.narration:

A filesystem UUID identifies the filesystem, not necessarily the underlying physical disk. Reformatting creates a new filesystem identity; cloning can copy an existing UUID and create ambiguity when both copies are attached.

Use direct, appropriately privileged probing when you need current metadata rather than relying on possibly incomplete cached information. After cloning or storage replacement, verify that persistent mount references identify exactly the intended filesystem. slides.title: 9.5 Partition Tables
keyPoints: A partition table describes regions of a disk assigned to partitions. It is separate from the filesystems inside those regions. Changing a partition boundary does not automatically transform or resize the filesystem it contains.
Linux example — 9.5
List partition layouts without writing them.
slides.narration:
A partition table describes regions of a disk assigned to partitions. It is separate from the filesystems inside those regions. Changing a partition boundary does not automatically transform or resize the filesystem it contains.

Preserve the starting sector of an existing filesystem when performing an approved growth operation. Moving the start is a different and much riskier task. Before changes, save the partition layout and ensure the backup is stored somewhere other than the device being modified.

For a new lab disk, plan alignment, boot requirements, data separation, and future growth. For an existing production disk, do not replace the table simply because a tool presents a cleaner-looking layout. The table is a map to existing data, not a cosmetic preference.

slides.title: 9.6 GPT and MBR
keyPoints: Use the format appropriate to the platform and operating-system requirements. Converting a live boot disk between schemes is a planned migration, not a routine command to try during an unrelated outage.
Linux example — 9.6
Inspect partition-table types.
slides.narration:
GPT is the modern partition-table format commonly paired with UEFI systems and supports more flexible partitioning than the older MBR scheme. MBR has historical size and partition-count limitations whose practical effect depends on sector size and layout.

GPT includes redundant metadata, but that does not make it a data backup. Corrupting a filesystem or losing the device is still a separate failure. Likewise, a valid partition table does not prove every partition contains a valid filesystem.

Use the format appropriate to the platform and operating-system requirements. Converting a live boot disk between schemes is a planned migration, not a routine command to try during an unrelated outage.

slides.title: 9.17 Filesystem Repair
keyPoints: Linux example — 9.17
Perform a nonwriting ext4 check on the unmounted image from 9.8.
What to check: Run only while the image is unmounted; -n refuses repairs and -f forces a check.
slides.narration:
Repair modifies filesystem metadata to recover a usable structure. It can discard damaged information and should not be treated as a harmless diagnostic. Prefer read-only assessment and a recoverable image or backup before destructive repair when feasible.

Use the filesystem-specific tool and its required mount state. ext4 checks normally use e2fsck on an unmounted filesystem. XFS repair uses xfs_repair on an unmounted filesystem; forcing log destruction is a high-risk last resort with possible data loss, not a default flag.

If storage hardware is failing, repeated scans may increase stress. Escalate to an appropriate recovery procedure and preserve the best available copy. A repaired filesystem also needs application-level validation: directory consistency does not prove a database is logically correct.

set -euo pipefail
lab_dir=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf -- "$lab_dir"' EXIT
cd -- "$lab_dir"
printf 'bytes_free=1048576\ninodes_free=0\n' > capacity.fixture
. ./capacity.fixture
test "$bytes_free" -gt 0 && test "$inodes_free" -eq 0
